newsitem.title: USA: Fla. judge strips tobacco of death benefit argument.
newsitem.headline: Fla. judge strips tobacco of death benefit argument.

text.p: A Florida judge told tobacco companies Wednesday they will not be allowed to argue to a jury that Florida saved money in its Medicaid programme because smokers die earlier than non-smokers.

Circuit Judge Harold Cohen said the industry will not be able to use the so-called "premature death benefit" to mitigate potential damages in the state's billion-dollar lawsuit, in which it seeks to recover money spent treating smoking-related illness.

The two sides were arguing final motions leading up to trial of the landmark case, in which the state alleges that tobacco companies should pay the cost of treating people with smoking-related illnesses. Jury selection was scheduled to begin Friday.

In their motion to present evidence on the "premature death benefit," the tobacco companies said: "Because smokers die younger on average than non-smokers, the former receive smaller Social Security payments and experience a briefer period of eligibility for Medicare services than the latter."
The industry concluded that "smokers subsidise non-smokers Social Security payments" because they cost the entire system less by dying early.
"If smokers cost less than non-smokers, then the jury should hear about it," argued Murray Garnick, an attorney for Philip Morris Cos. Inc.
W.C. Gentry, one of the attorneys for the state, said the idea of a premature death benefit credit was "abhorrent to civilised society."
"They are asking for a credit for killing people early," Gentry said.

Earlier Wednesday, the judge ruled that the cigarette companies cannot argue that Florida contributed to tobacco-related illness by failing to vigorously enforce laws against the sale of cigarettes to minors.

The tobacco companies had hoped to show evidence that Florida was partly to blame for such illnesses because it enforced laws barring gambling and alcohol consumption by minors but did little or nothing to halt the sale of cigarettes to children.
The judge again rejected the tobacco companies' attempt to introduce evidence that the state shared blame because it formerly made and distributed cigarettes in its prisons.

The judge said the information could not be used during the trial but could be considered in assessing damages if the tobacco companies are found guilty of misleading the public about the health risks of smoking.
